Diego Armando Maradona[A] (30 October 1960 – 25 November 2020) was an Argentine professional football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was an attacking midfielder renowned for his exceptional creativity, vision, passing, ball control, dribbling, and free-kick taking. A predominantly left-footed playmaker, he could also operate as a second striker. Nicknamed El Pibe de Oro ("The Golden Boy"), he was named one of the two winners of the FIFA Player of the Century award in 2000, alongside Pelé.

Born in Lanús and raised in Villa Fiorito, a villa miseria on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Maradona began his professional career with Argentinos Juniors in 1976, making his debut at the age of 15. He joined Boca Juniors in 1981 and helped the club win the 1981 Metropolitano championship. In 1982, he moved to Barcelona for a world-record transfer fee, winning the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Liga in 1983. He transferred to Napoli in 1984, breaking his own world transfer record. During his seven seasons in Italy, Maradona transformed Napoli into a major force in Italian and European football, leading the club to its first two Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990, as well as the Coppa Italia in 1987, the 1988–89 UEFA Cup and the Supercoppa Italiana in 1990. He later played for Sevilla and Newell's Old Boys before returning to Boca Juniors, where he retired in 1997.
At international level, Maradona made 91 appearances and scored 34 goals for Argentina between 1977 and 1994. After leading Argentina to the 1979 FIFA World Youth Championship title, he captained the senior team to victory at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico, scoring five goals, providing five assists and winning the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. In the quarter-final against England, he scored both goals in a 2–1 victory. The first, known as the "Hand of God", was scored illegally with his hand, while the second followed a solo run from inside his own half and was later voted the "Goal of the Century". He also scored both goals in the semi-final against Belgium and set up Jorge Burruchaga's winning goal against West Germany in the final. Maradona captained Argentina again at the 1990 World Cup, where they lost in the final. He went on to win the 1993 Artemio Franchi Cup, his last title.

Maradona struggled with drug addiction during his playing career. He received a 15-month suspension in 1991 after testing positive for cocaine and was excluded from the 1994 FIFA World Cup after testing positive for ephedrine. As a manager, he coached the Argentina national team from 2008 to 2010 and led them to the quarter-finals of the 2010 World Cup. He also managed clubs in the United Arab Emirates, Mexico and Argentina, ending his managerial career with Gimnasia de La Plata in 2020. Beyond his sporting achievements, Maradona became a cultural icon, particularly in Argentina and Naples; his popularity inspired religious devotion among some supporters, reflected in shrines and religious imagery dedicated to him. After his death in 2020, Argentina declared three days of national mourning, and Napoli's home stadium was renamed Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in his honour.
Early life
Maradona was born on 30 October 1960, at the Policlínico Evita Hospital in Lanús, Buenos Aires Province, to a poor Roman Catholic family. He was raised in Villa Fiorito, a shantytown on the southern outskirts of Buenos Aires.[3][4] His father, also named Diego Maradona, worked at a chemicals factory. His mother, Dalma Salvadora Franco, was of Italian and Croatian descent.[B] Maradona's parents grew up in Esquina in the north-east province of Corrientes, and moved to Buenos Aires in the 1950s.[4] Maradona's two younger brothers, Hugo and Raúl, both became professional footballers. He also had four older sisters.[10][11]

Maradona received his first football as a gift at age three and quickly became devoted to the game.[12] At age eight, he was spotted by a talent scout while he was playing at Estrella Roja, his local club. In March 1969, Maradona was recommended to Los Cebollitas (The Little Onions), the junior team of Buenos Aires's Argentinos Juniors club, by his friend Gregorio Carrizo, who had already been recruited by coach Francis Gregorio Cornejo.[13][14] Cornejo later remarked that the eight-year-old Maradona played football like an adult.[15] Maradona became a star for Los Cebollitas, and as a 12-year-old ball boy he entertained spectators with his ball skills during the halftime breaks of Argentinos Juniors' first division games.[16] During 1973 and 1974, Maradona led Los Cebollitas to two Evita Tournament victories and 141 undefeated games in a row, playing alongside Adrián Domenech and Claudio Rodríguez on what is regarded as the best youth team in the history of Argentine football.[17] Maradona named Brazilian playmaker Rivellino and Manchester United winger George Best among his inspirations growing up.[18][19]
Club career  
Argentinos Juniors  
Maradona (centre) performs a nutmeg during his debut in the Primera División on 20 October 1976.
On 20 October 1976, Maradona made his professional debut for Argentinos Juniors, ten days before his 16th birthday.[2][20] He became the youngest player in the history of the Argentine Primera División, and entered the match against Talleres de Córdoba wearing the number 16 jersey. A few minutes into the match, Maradona kicked the ball through the legs of Juan Domingo Cabrera, a nutmeg that would become symbolic of his talent.[21] After the game, Maradona said: "That day I felt I had held the sky in my hands."[22] Thirty years later, Cabrera recalled Maradona's debut: "I was on the right side of the field and went to press him, but he didn't give me a chance. He made the nutmeg and when I turned around, he was far away from me."[23]

Maradona scored his first two goals as a professional against the Marplatense club San Lorenzo on 14 November 1976, two weeks after turning 16.[24] He made 11 appearances in his debut season. During the 1977 season, he scored 19 goals in 49 matches, and began to attract the attention of other South American clubs. In the 1978 season, he scored 26 goals in 35 matches; to the surprise of many, he was not selected for the 1978 World Cup by coach César Luis Menotti.[25] In 1979, Maradona scored 26 goals in 26 games, and finished as the top scorer in both the Metropolitan and Nacional tournaments. In 1980, he scored 43 goals in 45 appearances and was the top scorer during four consecutive tournaments.[26] In total, Maradona spent five years at Argentinos Juniors, scoring 116 goals in 166 appearances.
Boca Juniors  
Maradona being held aloft by Boca Juniors supporters after winning the 1981 Metropolitano title
Maradona completed a US$4-million transfer to the Argentine club Boca Juniors in February 1981.[27] He had received offers from other clubs, including River Plate, which offered to make him their highest paid player.[28] However, River ultimately dropped their bid due to their large payroll and desire to retain Daniel Passarella and Ubaldo Fillol.[29] Maradona made his debut for Boca on 22 February against Talleres de Córdoba, scoring twice in a 4–1 win. On 10 April, he played his first Superclásico against River Plate at La Bombonera stadium. Boca defeated River 3–0 with Maradona scoring once.[30] Despite the distrustful relationship between Maradona and Boca Juniors manager Silvio Marzolini,[31] Boca won the 1981 league title.[32]
Barcelona  
Maradona (right) and fellow Argentine Mario Kempes before a 1982 match between Barcelona and Valencia

In 1982, Maradona transferred to Barcelona for a then-world record fee of £5 million ($7.6 million).[33] According to Barcelona player Lobo Carrasco, Maradona's teammates were so amazed by his ball control that they simply stood by and watched him dribble during an early training session.[34] Maradona's encouraging first season at Barça was disrupted in December 1982 when he was diagnosed with hepatitis B, which sidelined him for nearly three months.[35] He returned to action on 12 March 1983 against Real Betis, coinciding with the debut of César Luis Menotti as Barcelona's manager.[36] Under Menotti, Barcelona won the Copa del Rey and the Copa de la Liga, defeating their longtime rivals Real Madrid in both tournaments.[37] In the final of the Copa del Rey, Maradona assisted Víctor Muñoz's goal in a 2–1 win.[37] In the first leg of the Copa de la Liga finals at Estadio Santiago Bernabéu in Madrid, he assisted Carrasco's goal and then scored one himself as the game ended in a 2–2 draw.[37] Maradona became the first Barcelona player to receive a standing ovation at the Bernabéu.[C] Three days later, Barcelona won the second leg against Real Madrid 2–1, with Maradona scoring from a penalty kick.[37] On 24 September 1983, a tackle by Andoni Goikoetxea of Athletic Bilbao fractured Maradona's left ankle and tore its medial ligament.[41] The injury required surgery later that night and raised fears for his playing career.[42] He was sidelined for three and a half months, missing both legs of the 1983 Supercopa de España.[35][36][42]

Maradona married his long-time fiancée Claudia Villafañe on 7 November 1989 in Buenos Aires.[263] They had two daughters, Dalma Nerea (born in 1987) and Gianinna Dinorah (born in 1989). Gianinna married Argentine footballer Sergio Agüero and gave birth to Maradona's grandson, Benjamín.[264][265] Maradona and Villafañe divorced in 2004. According to Dalma Nerea, her parents remained on friendly terms. They travelled together to Naples for a series of homages in June 2005 and were seen together at the 2006 World Cup.[266] During the divorce proceedings, Maradona admitted that he was the father of Diego Sinagra, who was born in Naples in 1986. Diego Sinagra met Maradona for the first time in May 2003 after tricking his way onto a golf course in Italy where Maradona was playing.[267] Sinagra played professional football until 2020.[268] Maradona's mother died on 19 November 2011 at age 81, and his father died on 25 June 2015 at age 87.[269]
In 2014, Maradona denied allegations that he assaulted his girlfriend, Rocío Oliva.[270][271] In 2017, he bought her a house in Bella Vista, and in 2018 they separated.[272] Maradona's great-nephew Hernán López is also a professional footballer.[273]
Health
From the mid-1980s until 2004, Maradona was addicted to cocaine. He allegedly began using the drug in Barcelona in 1983.[274] By the time he was playing for Napoli, the addiction was interfering with his ability to play football.[275] Maradona was banned from football in both 1991 and 1994 for abusing drugs.[276]

Maradona had a tendency to put on weight and suffered increasingly from obesity, at one point weighing 280 lb (130 kg). He was obese from the end of his playing career until undergoing gastric bypass surgery in a clinic in Cartagena, Colombia, on 6 March 2005. His surgeon said that Maradona would follow a liquid diet for three months in order to return to his normal weight.[277] When Maradona resumed public appearances shortly thereafter, he displayed a notably thinner figure.[278]
At the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia, Maradona was seen behaving erratically. He then collapsed and was treated by paramedics.
On 29 March 2007, Maradona was treated for hepatitis and effects of alcohol abuse at a hospital in Buenos Aires. He was released on 11 April, then readmitted two days later.[279] In the following days, there were constant rumours about his health, including three false claims of his death within a month.[280] After being transferred to a psychiatric clinic specialising in alcohol-related problems, Maradona was discharged on 7 May.[281] The following day, Maradona appeared on Argentine television and stated that he had quit drinking and had not used drugs in two and a half years.[282] During the 2018 World Cup match between Argentina and Nigeria, Maradona was seen behaving erratically.[283] Following the match, he collapsed and was treated by paramedics; he later attributed his behaviour to consumption of wine.[284] In January 2019, he underwent surgery after a hernia caused internal bleeding in his stomach.[285]
In 2026, during the trial of Maradona's medical team for medical negligence, Maradona's psychologist Carlos Diaz stated that he had been diagnosed with both bipolar disorder and narcissistic personality disorder during his lifetime.[286]
Political views  
Maradona (right) presenting a signed jersey to the former President of Argentina Néstor Kirchner in December 2007.

Maradona was ideologically left-wing.[287] He supported the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and condemned Israel's military strikes in the Gaza Strip during the 2014 Israel–Gaza conflict, saying: "What Israel is doing to the Palestinians is shameful."[288] He became friends with Cuban president Fidel Castro while receiving treatment on the island, with Castro stating, "Diego is a great friend and very noble, too. There's also no question he's a wonderful athlete and has maintained a friendship with Cuba to no material gain of his own."[89] Maradona had a portrait of Castro tattooed on his left leg and one of Fidel's second in command, fellow Argentine Che Guevara on his right arm.[186] In his autobiography, El Diego, he dedicated the book to various people, including Castro. He wrote: "To Fidel Castro and, through him, all the Cuban people."[289] In 1990, he visited Lenin's Mausoleum in Red Square.[290]
"I'm convinced that if he hadn't been a footballer, he'd've become a revolutionary."
— Filmmaker Emir Kusturica, on Maradona[89]
Maradona voiced support for Bolivia's president Evo Morales[291] and was also a supporter of former Venezuelan president Hugo Chávez. In 2005, he came to Venezuela to meet Chávez, who received him in the presidential Miraflores Palace. After the meeting, Maradona said that he had come to meet a "great man" (un grande, which can also mean "a big man", in Spanish), but had instead met a gigantic man (un gigante). He also stated, "I believe in Chávez, I am a Chavista. Everything Fidel does, everything Chávez does, for me is the best."[292] Maradona was Chávez's guest of honour at the opening game of the 2007 Copa América held in Venezuela.[293] In a 2017 interview, Maradona praised Russian president Vladimir Putin and considered him, along with Chavez and Castro, to be among the best political leaders in the world, stating: "Putin is a man who can bring peace to many in this world. He's a phenomenon; simply a phenomenon".[294]

In senior club and international football, Maradona made a combined 680 appearances and scored 345 goals, averaging 0.51 goals per match.[O]

After leading Argentina to the 1979 FIFA World Youth Championship title, he captained the senior team to victory at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico, scoring five goals, providing five assists and winning the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. In the quarter-final against England, he scored both goals in a 2–1 victory. The first, known as the "Hand of God", was scored illegally with his hand, while the second followed a solo run from inside his own half and was later voted the "Goal of the Century". He also scored both goals in the semi-final against Belgium and set up Jorge Burruchaga's winning goal against West Germany in the final. texts.3:
Maradona struggled with drug addiction during his playing career. He received a 15-month suspension in 1991 after testing positive for cocaine and was excluded from the 1994 FIFA World Cup after testing positive for ephedrine. As a manager, he coached the Argentina national team from 2008 to 2010 and led them to the quarter-finals of the 2010 World Cup. He also managed clubs in the United Arab Emirates, Mexico and Argentina, ending his managerial career with Gimnasia de La Plata in 2020. Beyond his sporting achievements, Maradona became a cultural icon, particularly in Argentina and Naples; his popularity inspired religious devotion among some supporters, reflected in shrines and religious imagery dedicated to him. After his death in 2020, Argentina declared three days of national mourning, and Napoli's home stadium was renamed Stadio Diego Armando Maradona in his honour.
Early life
Maradona was born on 30 October 1960, at the Policlínico Evita Hospital in Lanús, Buenos Aires Province, to a poor Roman Catholic family. He was raised in Villa Fiorito, a shantytown on the southern outskirts of Buenos Aires.[3][4] His father, also named Diego Maradona, worked at a chemicals factory. His mother, Dalma Salvadora Franco, was of Italian and Croatian descent.[B] Maradona's parents grew up in Esquina in the north-east province of Corrientes, and moved to Buenos Aires in the 1950s.[4] Maradona's two younger brothers, Hugo and Raúl, both became professional footballers. He also had four older sisters.[10][11]
texts.4:
Maradona received his first football as a gift at age three and quickly became devoted to the game.[12] At age eight, he was spotted by a talent scout while he was playing at Estrella Roja, his local club. In March 1969, Maradona was recommended to Los Cebollitas (The Little Onions), the junior team of Buenos Aires's Argentinos Juniors club, by his friend Gregorio Carrizo, who had already been recruited by coach Francis Gregorio Cornejo.[13][14] Cornejo later remarked that the eight-year-old Maradona played football like an adult.[15] Maradona became a star for Los Cebollitas, and as a 12-year-old ball boy he entertained spectators with his ball skills during the halftime breaks of Argentinos Juniors' first division games.[16] During 1973 and 1974, Maradona led Los Cebollitas to two Evita Tournament victories and 141 undefeated games in a row, playing alongside Adrián Domenech and Claudio Rodríguez on what is regarded as the best youth team in the history of Argentine football.[17] Maradona named Brazilian playmaker Rivellino and Manchester United winger George Best among his inspirations growing up.[18][19]
Club career  
Argentinos Juniors  
Maradona (centre) performs a nutmeg during his debut in the Primera División on 20 October 1976.
On 20 October 1976, Maradona made his professional debut for Argentinos Juniors, ten days before his 16th birthday.[2][20] He became the youngest player in the history of the Argentine Primera División, and entered the match against Talleres de Córdoba wearing the number 16 jersey. A few minutes into the match, Maradona kicked the ball through the legs of Juan Domingo Cabrera, a nutmeg that would become symbolic of his talent.[21] After the game, Maradona said: "That day I felt I had held the sky in my hands."[22] Thirty years later, Cabrera recalled Maradona's debut: "I was on the right side of the field and went to press him, but he didn't give me a chance. He made the nutmeg and when I turned around, he was far away from me."[23]
texts.5:
Maradona scored his first two goals as a professional against the Marplatense club San Lorenzo on 14 November 1976, two weeks after turning 16.[24] He made 11 appearances in his debut season. During the 1977 season, he scored 19 goals in 49 matches, and began to attract the attention of other South American clubs. In the 1978 season, he scored 26 goals in 35 matches; to the surprise of many, he was not selected for the 1978 World Cup by coach César Luis Menotti.[25] In 1979, Maradona scored 26 goals in 26 games, and finished as the top scorer in both the Metropolitan and Nacional tournaments. In 1980, he scored 43 goals in 45 appearances and was the top scorer during four consecutive tournaments.[26] In total, Maradona spent five years at Argentinos Juniors, scoring 116 goals in 166 appearances.
Boca Juniors  
Maradona being held aloft by Boca Juniors supporters after winning the 1981 Metropolitano title
Maradona completed a US$4-million transfer to the Argentine club Boca Juniors in February 1981.[27] He had received offers from other clubs, including River Plate, which offered to make him their highest paid player.[28] However, River ultimately dropped their bid due to their large payroll and desire to retain Daniel Passarella and Ubaldo Fillol.[29] Maradona made his debut for Boca on 22 February against Talleres de Córdoba, scoring twice in a 4–1 win. On 10 April, he played his first Superclásico against River Plate at La Bombonera stadium. Boca defeated River 3–0 with Maradona scoring once.[30] Despite the distrustful relationship between Maradona and Boca Juniors manager Silvio Marzolini,[31] Boca won the 1981 league title.[32]
Barcelona  
Maradona (right) and fellow Argentine Mario Kempes before a 1982 match between Barcelona and Valencia
texts.6: In 1982, Maradona transferred to Barcelona for a then-world record fee of £5 million ($7.6 million).[33] According to Barcelona player Lobo Carrasco, Maradona's teammates were so amazed by his ball control that they simply stood by and watched him dribble during an early training session.[34] Maradona's encouraging first season at Barça was disrupted in December 1982 when he was diagnosed with hepatitis B, which sidelined him for nearly three months.[35] He returned to action on 12 March 1983 against Real Betis, coinciding with the debut of César Luis Menotti as Barcelona's manager.[36] Under Menotti, Barcelona won the Copa del Rey and the Copa de la Liga, defeating their longtime rivals Real Madrid in both tournaments.[37] In the final of the Copa del Rey, Maradona assisted Víctor Muñoz's goal in a 2–1 win.[37] In the first leg of the Copa de la Liga finals at Estadio Santiago Bernabéu in Madrid, he assisted Carrasco's goal and then scored one himself as the game ended in a 2–2 draw.[37] Maradona became the first Barcelona player to receive a standing ovation at the Bernabéu.[C] Three days later, Barcelona won the second leg against Real Madrid 2–1, with Maradona scoring from a penalty kick.[37] On 24 September 1983, a tackle by Andoni Goikoetxea of Athletic Bilbao fractured Maradona's left ankle and tore its medial ligament.[41] The injury required surgery later that night and raised fears for his playing career.[42] He was sidelined for three and a half months, missing both legs of the 1983 Supercopa de España.[35][36][42]

Maradona married his long-time fiancée Claudia Villafañe on 7 November 1989 in Buenos Aires.[263] They had two daughters, Dalma Nerea (born in 1987) and Gianinna Dinorah (born in 1989). Gianinna married Argentine footballer Sergio Agüero and gave birth to Maradona's grandson, Benjamín.[264][265] Maradona and Villafañe divorced in 2004. According to Dalma Nerea, her parents remained on friendly terms. They travelled together to Naples for a series of homages in June 2005 and were seen together at the 2006 World Cup.[266] During the divorce proceedings, Maradona admitted that he was the father of Diego Sinagra, who was born in Naples in 1986. Diego Sinagra met Maradona for the first time in May 2003 after tricking his way onto a golf course in Italy where Maradona was playing.[267] Sinagra played professional football until 2020.[268] Maradona's mother died on 19 November 2011 at age 81, and his father died on 25 June 2015 at age 87.[269]
In 2014, Maradona denied allegations that he assaulted his girlfriend, Rocío Oliva.[270][271] In 2017, he bought her a house in Bella Vista, and in 2018 they separated.[272] Maradona's great-nephew Hernán López is also a professional footballer.[273]
Health
From the mid-1980s until 2004, Maradona was addicted to cocaine. He allegedly began using the drug in Barcelona in 1983.[274] By the time he was playing for Napoli, the addiction was interfering with his ability to play football.[275] Maradona was banned from football in both 1991 and 1994 for abusing drugs.[276]
texts.32:
Maradona had a tendency to put on weight and suffered increasingly from obesity, at one point weighing 280 lb (130 kg). He was obese from the end of his playing career until undergoing gastric bypass surgery in a clinic in Cartagena, Colombia, on 6 March 2005. His surgeon said that Maradona would follow a liquid diet for three months in order to return to his normal weight.[277] When Maradona resumed public appearances shortly thereafter, he displayed a notably thinner figure.[278]
At the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia, Maradona was seen behaving erratically. He then collapsed and was treated by paramedics.
On 29 March 2007, Maradona was treated for hepatitis and effects of alcohol abuse at a hospital in Buenos Aires. In 2026, during the trial of Maradona's medical team for medical negligence, Maradona's psychologist Carlos Diaz stated that he had been diagnosed with both bipolar disorder and narcissistic personality disorder during his lifetime.[286]
Political views  
Maradona (right) presenting a signed jersey to the former President of Argentina Néstor Kirchner in December 2007.
texts.33:
Maradona was ideologically left-wing.[287] He supported the establishment of an independent Palestinian state and condemned Israel's military strikes in the Gaza Strip during the 2014 Israel–Gaza conflict, saying: "What Israel is doing to the Palestinians is shameful."[288] He became friends with Cuban president Fidel Castro while receiving treatment on the island, with Castro stating, "Diego is a great friend and very noble, too. There's also no question he's a wonderful athlete and has maintained a friendship with Cuba to no material gain of his own."[89] Maradona had a portrait of Castro tattooed on his left leg and one of Fidel's second in command, fellow Argentine Che Guevara on his right arm.[186] In his autobiography, El Diego, he dedicated the book to various people, including Castro. He wrote: "To Fidel Castro and, through him, all the Cuban people."[289] In 1990, he visited Lenin's Mausoleum in Red Square.[290]
"I'm convinced that if he hadn't been a footballer, he'd've become a revolutionary."
— Filmmaker Emir Kusturica, on Maradona[89]
Maradona voiced support for Bolivia's president Evo Morales[291] and was also a supporter of former Venezuelan president Hugo Chávez. In 2005, he came to Venezuela to meet Chávez, who received him in the presidential Miraflores Palace. After the meeting, Maradona said that he had come to meet a "great man" (un grande, which can also mean "a big man", in Spanish), but had instead met a gigantic man (un gigante). He also stated, "I believe in Chávez, I am a Chavista. Everything Fidel does, everything Chávez does, for me is the best."[292] Maradona was Chávez's guest of honour at the opening game of the 2007 Copa América held in Venezuela.[293] In a 2017 interview, Maradona praised Russian president Vladimir Putin and considered him, along with Chavez and Castro, to be among the best political leaders in the world, stating: "Putin is a man who can bring peace to many in this world. He's a phenomenon; simply a phenomenon".[294]
